memories.content: Link expected participant burden in each user study task to its corresponding mitigation strategy.
Specify the accommodations necessary for participants to access the prototype and research tasks.
Specify how accessibility accommodations will be provided during user study sessions.
Describe how personal identifiers will be separated from research data immediately after collection.
Specify the equipment to be loaned to participants who lack necessary devices.
Describe the procedure for returning equipment loaned to participants.
HCI ethics reviewers verify that expected burdens and mitigation strategies correspond to each user study task.
Inform participants that the formative evaluation prototype is not a finished service.
Set an upper limit on cumulative task burden when requesting repeated evaluations from the same participant.
The author of this proposal tends to emphasize expected benefits of the prototype over participant burden.
In organizations where leaders or institutional staff handle recruitment, recruitment authority and academic or professional evaluation authority may be combined in the same role.
Link anticipated participant burden with its mitigation strategies for each field user study task.
Specify the accommodations necessary for participants to access the field system and research tasks.
Specify how accessibility accommodations will be provided in the field user study.
Describe how personal identifiers will be separated from research data immediately upon collection.
List equipment to be loaned when participants lack necessary gear.
Describe the procedure for returning equipment loaned to participants.
The HCI ethics reviewer verifies that anticipated burden and mitigation strategies correspond for each field user study task.
Ensure that participants can safely return to existing work procedures if they discontinue research participation.
Specify that organizational members who decline research participation will not face disadvantages in task assignment or performance evaluation.
The user's withdrawal risk can be adequately assessed only when a safe alternative procedure exists for field tasks.
The user tends to assume that a short session also entails little burden from work interruption and exposure to a manager.

analysis.overview: The frames align on core ethics documentation for burden, accessibility, data separation, equipment, and review, with several claims narrowed to field-study contexts. Each side also contributes independent safeguards and observations concerning prototypes, repeated participation, authority, withdrawal, workplace consequences, and burden underestimation.

relations.reason: The operational requirement is shared, but the field-study condition materially narrows where the compared formulation governs.
relations.summary: Both require task-level linkage between anticipated participant burden and mitigation strategies, with the compared claim explicitly limited to field user studies.

relations.reason: The access requirement aligns, while the explicit prototype-versus-field-system setting must be preserved.
relations.summary: Both require specification of accommodations needed to access the studied system and research tasks, with prototype access in the reference and field-system access in the compared frame.

relations.reason: The same delivery-planning obligation is expressed under different explicit study settings.
relations.summary: Both require specification of how accessibility accommodations will be delivered, during study sessions generally in the reference and during a field user study in the compared frame.

relations.reason: The formulations state the same operational privacy requirement under the same relevant scope.
relations.summary: Both require personal identifiers to be separated from research data immediately upon collection.

relations.reason: The wording differs without changing the equipment-identification obligation or its triggering condition.
relations.summary: Both require specifying equipment to loan participants who lack necessary devices or gear.
Both require a procedure for returning equipment loaned to participants.

relations.reason: The review duty aligns, but the compared frame's field-study scope is a material condition.
relations.summary: Both assign HCI ethics reviewers responsibility for verifying task-level correspondence between burden and mitigation, with the compared claim explicitly limited to field user studies.

relations.reason: This disclosure obligation is independently useful and has no counterpart in the compared frame.
relations.summary: The reference requires informing participants that the formative-evaluation prototype is not a finished service.

relations.reason: This repeated-participation safeguard is independently useful and absent from the compared frame.
relations.summary: The reference requires an upper limit on cumulative task burden for repeated evaluations by the same participant.

relations.reason: This author-specific assessment bias is independently useful and is not restated by the compared frame.
relations.summary: The reference observes that the proposal author tends to emphasize expected prototype benefits over participant burden.

relations.reason: This structural authority concern is independently useful and has no corresponding claim in the compared frame.
relations.summary: The reference notes that recruitment authority and academic or professional evaluation authority may be combined in one organizational role.

relations.reason: This withdrawal safeguard is independently useful and has no counterpart in the reference frame.
relations.summary: The compared frame requires participants who discontinue research participation to be able to return safely to existing work procedures.

relations.reason: This protection against workplace consequences is independently useful and absent from the reference frame.
relations.summary: The compared frame requires assurance that organizational members declining participation suffer no disadvantage in task assignment or performance evaluation.

relations.reason: This condition on adequate risk assessment is independently useful and distinct from the reference content.
relations.summary: The compared frame states that withdrawal risk can be adequately assessed only when a safe alternative procedure exists for field tasks.

relations.reason: This specific burden-underestimation bias is independently useful and is not equivalent to the reference frame's author-specific benefit emphasis.
relations.summary: The compared frame observes a tendency to infer low burden from a short session despite work interruption and manager exposure.

reports.both: Both require immediate identifier separation, equipment specification and return procedures, alongside closely aligned burden, accommodation, and ethics-review practices.
reports.compared_only: The compared frame adds safe withdrawal procedures, protection from workplace disadvantage, a condition for assessing withdrawal risk, and concern that short sessions may still impose workplace burdens.
reports.differences: Several shared practices are explicitly framed around field systems and field studies on the compared side, while the reference wording applies more generally or to prototypes and sessions.
reports.reference_only: The reference adds prototype-status disclosure, cumulative burden limits, benefit-over-burden bias, and risks from combined recruitment and evaluation authority.
